facts.statement: The scientific name of the extinct animal is Eremosuchus.
facts.quote: taxon: Eremosuchus

facts.statement: Eremosuchus lived during the Ypresian stage of the Eocene epoch.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Eocene (Ypresian)

facts.statement: Eremosuchus was first described by Buffetaut in 1989.
facts.quote: authority: Buffetaut, 1989

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Eremosuchus is E. elkoholicus.
facts.quote: type_species: E. elkoholicus

facts.statement: Eremosuchus is a genus of sebecosuchian notosuchian found in the Early Eocene El Kohol Formation of Algeria.
facts.quote: Eremosuchus is an extinct genus of sebecosuchian notosuchian from the Early Eocene El Kohol Formation of Algeria.

facts.statement: Eremosuchus was first described based on isolated cranial and postcranial material in 1989.
facts.quote: It was first described on the basis of isolated cranial and postcranial material in 1989

facts.statement: Eremosuchus possessed serrated, blade-like teeth known as ziphodonty.
facts.quote: Like other sebecids it had serrated, blade-like teeth, a condition referred to as ziphodonty.

facts.statement: Eremosuchus is currently the only named sebecid known from Africa.
facts.quote: It is currently the only named sebecid from Africa.

facts.statement: Fossil remains of Eremosuchus were discovered in 1982 at the El Kohol site in northern Algeria by researchers from the Université d'Oran, Sorbonne Universités, and Université de Montpellier.
facts.quote: The first fossil remains of Eremosuchus were discovered by the combined efforts of the Université d'Oran, Sorbonne Universités and Université de Montpellier in 1982 at the El Kohol site in northern Algeria

facts.statement: The holotype of Eremosuchus is the dentary bone designated UO-KB-301.
facts.quote: the dentary (UO-KB-301) serving as the holotype of the new genus Eremosuchus

facts.statement: Cecily S. C. Nicholl and colleagues published a redescription of Eremosuchus in 2025.
facts.quote: In 2025 Cecily S. C. Nicholl and colleagues published an in-depth redescription of Eremosuchus

facts.statement: The holotype dentary of Eremosuchus is a slender bone measuring 156 mm in total length.
facts.quote: The dentary of Eremosuchus is a slender bone significantly narrower than it is high and measures a total of 156 mm in the presumably adult holotype specimen.

facts.statement: The two halves of the lower jaw diverged at an angle of about 10 to 15 degrees.
facts.quote: Based on the preserved right dentary the two halves of the lower jaw would have diverged at an angle of about 10 - 15°

facts.statement: The dentary reaches a maximum height of at least 50 mm at the fourth tooth.
facts.quote: The height of the dentary initially increases from the tip of the lower jaw to the enlarged fourth dentary tooth, where the bone reaches its maximum height of at least 50 mm.

facts.statement: The surface of the dentary features varying types of ornamentation including grooves and pits.
facts.quote: The surface of the dentary is marked by varying types of ornamentation.

facts.statement: The surangular bone is expanded towards the top and thins towards its ventral contact with the angular bone.
facts.quote: The surangular is described as being expanded towards the top, thinning towards its ventral contact with the angular.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis suggests Eremosuchus is closely related to terrestrial members of Sebecidae from South America, though results are inconclusive.
facts.quote: Phylogenetic analysis conducted using Eremosuchus material yield inconclusive results, but overall support a close relationship with the terrestrial members of Sebecidae best known from the Cenozoic of South America

facts.statement: It is debated whether Eremosuchus's lineage split off during sebecid dispersal between South America and Europe, or if ancestors arrived in North Africa from Europe via the Tethys Sea.
facts.quote: It is possible that the lineage leading to Eremosuchus split off as sebecids dispersed between South America and Europe or that its ancestors arrived in North Africa from Europe after crossing the Tethys sea.

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Eremosuchus contains 12 tooth sockets representing the full tooth row.
facts.quote: The dentary of Eremosuchus preserves a total of 12 alveoli, which likely represent the entirety of the mandibular tooth row.

facts.statement: The front teeth of Eremosuchus are angled forward (procumbent) due to the forward orientation of their sockets.
facts.quote: The anterior teeth are further set apart from those further back in the jaw by their orientation, being procumbent thanks to the more anterior orientation of the alveoli.

facts.statement: Thin bony walls separate the individual tooth sockets in the lower jaw of Eremosuchus.
facts.quote: Each alveolus is separated from its neighbors by a thin septum.

facts.statement: A gap in the tooth row (diastema) follows the seventh socket in a juvenile specimen of Eremosuchus, but this gap is absent in the adult holotype.
facts.quote: The seventh alveolus in the referred specimen is then immediately followed by a diastema that is not present in the holotype.

facts.statement: The fourth tooth of Eremosuchus is slightly compressed but retains a classic canine shape with thinning edges.
facts.quote: The fourth tooth was comparably more compressed but nonetheless retained a classic caniniform morphology and possessed thinning distal and medial edges.

facts.statement: The tooth sockets behind the fourth tooth in Eremosuchus are uniform in size, with diameters between 8 and 11 mm.
facts.quote: The alveoli following the fourth caniniform tooth on the other hand are fairly uniform in size, their diameter only ranging between 8-11 mm.

facts.statement: The teeth of Eremosuchus have serrated cutting edges and are compressed, classifying them as ziphodont.
facts.quote: The cutting edges or carinae of these teeth bear symmetrical denticles, giving the teeth a pronounced serration that together with the labiolingual compression qualifies them as ziphodont.

facts.statement: Teeth preserved in the jaw of Eremosuchus have smooth enamel at the base and wrinkled enamel at the tip, lacking ridges or wear facets.
facts.quote: The enamel of the teeth found still in situ in the jaw bones is described as smooth towards the base of the crown but more wrinkled towards the apex with no signs of a wear facet or apicobasal ridges.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the variation in tooth enamel ornamentation found in Eremosuchus might be due to individual or species-level variation rather than distinct species.
facts.quote: However Nicholl and colleagues highlight that the specific ornamentation of the tooth enamel can vary among species and even individuals, with Eremosuchus possibly being an example of this.

facts.statement: The lower half of the fibula in Eremosuchus curves backward, a unique feature not found in other sebecids or baurusuchids.
facts.quote: The distal half of the fibula is bowed towards the back, a feature unique to Eremosuchus not seen in other sebecids or baurusuchids.

facts.statement: The vertebrae of Eremosuchus are amphicoelous, and the dorsal vertebrae are described as having a rounded bottom edge and a noticeable narrowing.
facts.quote: All vertebrae are amphicoelous as is the norm among notosuchians, but the only additional description provided for the dorsals suggests they had a rounded ventral edge and a marked constriction.

facts.statement: The tail vertebrae of Eremosuchus feature prominent parallel ridges on the underside covering about one-third of the centrum's length.
facts.quote: Both known tail vertebrae preserve a pair of low parallel ridges on their underside located at approximately the midpoint and covering about a third of the length of the vertebral centrum.

facts.statement: The tail vertebrae of Eremosuchus are relatively more elongated compared to their height than those of baurusuchids.
facts.quote: However, the centra of Eremosuchus′ tail vertebrae differ from those of baurusuchids in their exact proportions, being relatively more elongated compared to their height.

facts.statement: Isolated osteoderms found at the El Kohol locality in Algeria may have belonged to Eremosuchus, though they were not specifically assigned to it by the original describer.
facts.quote: The El Kohol locality in Algeria has also yielded some isolated osteoderms, which although not specifically referred to Eremosuchus by Buffetaut may have belonged to this taxon.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Eremosuchus uniquely possessed multiple types of osteoderm ornamentation, if only one type belongs to the species, or if neither type belongs to Eremosuchus.
facts.quote: Nicholl and colleagues propose three possible answers to this issue: either Eremosuchus was unique among notosuchians for featuring more than one type of dorsal osteoderm ornamentation, only one osteoderm type actually belonged to this taxon while the other represents a distinct second form or neither osteoderm type actually belonged to Eremosuchus.

facts.statement: In 1989, Eric Buffetaut classified Eremosuchus in the family Trematochampsidae.
facts.quote: By the time Buffetaut published the full description of Eremosuchus in 1989 he had come to refer it to the family Trematochampsidae

facts.statement: Later studies argued that the family Trematochampsidae is not a valid clade.
facts.quote: However, later studies eventually argued that Trematochampsidae was not a valid clade

facts.statement: Turner and Calvo argued that the features used to assign Eremosuchus to Trematochampsidae were of questionable value.
facts.quote: Turner and Calvo argued that the assignment to this family was based on a few cranial features of questionable value

facts.statement: Several phylogenetic analyses have recovered Eremosuchus as closely related to the clade Sebecosuchia.
facts.quote: Furthermore, several publications that included Eremosuchus in their phylogenetic analysis recovered it as more closely related to the clade Sebecosuchia

facts.statement: In 1996, Ortega and colleagues proposed a close relationship between Eremosuchus and Baurusuchus.
facts.quote: Ortega and colleagues, who proposed a close relationship to Baurusuchus in 1996

facts.statement: In 2005, Turner and Calvo recovered Eremosuchus as an early branching sebecosuchian.
facts.quote: followed by Turner and Calvo who recovered it as an early branching sebecosuchian in 2005

facts.statement: In 2013, Montefeltro regarded Eremosuchus as a baurusuchid.
facts.quote: Montefeltro who again regarded it as a baurusuchid in 2013

facts.statement: A 2025 study by Bravo and colleagues found conflicting results, recovering Eremosuchus as either closely related to baurusuchids or sebecoids.
facts.quote: In a 2025 study Bravo and colleagues recovered multiple possible outcomes including both a closer relationship to baurusuchids and one closer to sebecoids

facts.statement: The 2025 redescription of Eremosuchus consistently placed it as a sebecoid rather than a baurusuchid, despite some conflicting results.
facts.quote: the 2025 redescription yielded somewhat conflicting results, though they consistently regard Eremosuchus as being a sebecoid rather than a baurusuchid

facts.statement: Nicholl and colleagues noted that Eremosuchus shares features with sebecids but lacks features exclusive to baurusuchids.
facts.quote: Nicholl and colleagues highlight that while Eremosuchus shares several features seen in some or even all sebecids, it does not present any features exclusive to baurusuchids

facts.statement: Eremosuchus is the only named sebecid from continental Africa and may link South American and European taxa.
facts.quote: As the only named sebecid from continental Africa Eremosuchus may be a significant link between the taxa of South America and those of Europe

facts.statement: It is unclear whether Eremosuchus represents an African lineage linking South America and Europe or a descendant of a European form that moved into northern Africa.
facts.quote: Because of this it remains unclear whether Eremosuchus is part of an African lineage that directly links the taxa of South America and Europe or if it instead represents a descendant of a European form that crossed the Tethys southward into northern Africa

facts.statement: Due to a poor fossil record in key Cretaceous deposits, the origin of sebecoids in Europe or Africa cannot be excluded.
facts.quote: Nicholl and colleagues concede that given the poor fossil record of Cretaceous sebecids, which is conspicuously absent from key deposits like the Bauru Group of South America and the Kem Kem Beds of North Africa, a European or African origin cannot be excluded
